also: come and sit up at the table

evidence: Ter. Eun. 459: eāmus ergō ad cēnam. quid stās?
terms.comment: What Terence’s soldier says when it is time to eat: let us go to dinner, and why are you standing there? At home it is the call to the table; for the midday meal, ad prandium.

terms.gloss: come and eat (a morning or midday meal)
terms.comment: The risen Lord’s words to the disciples on the shore, with fish and bread at daybreak.

evidence: Ter. Haut. 124: adsīdō: adcurrunt servī, soccōs dētrahunt
terms.comment: The Romans lay at table (see “recline at table”); for sitting down on a chair at a table, Traupman’s mēnsae assīdere, or simply ad mēnsam cōnsīde (see “sit down”). In Terence a father comes home and sits down while the slaves run to take off his shoes and get dinner ready.

phrases.latin: Eāmus ergō ad cēnam. Quid stās?
phrases.english: Let’s go to dinner, then. Why are you standing there?

phrases.latin: tempusque esse coeperat edendī et tacendī
phrases.english: and it was time to eat and stop talking

phrases.latin: Age, mēnsae assīde: cēna parāta est.
phrases.english: Come on, sit down at the table: dinner’s ready.

sources: Lewis & Short: cena · Lewis & Short: prandeo · Lewis & Short: assido
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 389.
